claims.text: Cast equiatomic or near-equiatomic Nb-Mo-Ta-W-V has grains larger than 10 μm, a single-phase BCC structure, and limited room-temperature ductility.
Cryogenic HPT or ECAP can refine Nb-Mo-Ta-W-V to a grain size below 50 nm.
Annealing the deformed alloy at 400-600 °C can transform it into a dual-phase BCC/FCC solid solution without ordered intermetallics.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the BCC/FCC structure and prevents long-range ordering.
Severe plastic deformation produces nanocrystalline grains through dislocation accumulation, grain subdivision, and dynamic recrystallization.
The single-phase BCC Nb-Mo-Ta-W-V solid solution is thermodynamically unstable at low temperature and consequently separates into BCC and FCC phases.
B2 and Laves phases require long-range ordering or favorable local stoichiometry.
Nanocrystalline grain boundaries increase strength through Hall-Petch strengthening.
BCC/FCC phase boundaries provide additional strengthening.
The FCC phase improves ductility by supplying additional slip systems.
The proposed route will produce an average grain size of 30-45 nm.
The processed alloy will contain approximately equal volume fractions of BCC and FCC phases.
The processed alloy will have a yield strength above 1.5 GPa.
The processed alloy will have compressive ductility above 10%.
The processed alloy will have hardness above 600 HV.
As-cast Nb-Mo-Ta-W-V has a yield strength of approximately 1.0 GPa and ductility below 5%.
Annealing above 0.4 Tm causes rapid coarsening of the nanocrystalline structure.
Annealing above 0.5 Tm destabilizes the dual-phase solid solution and can promote B2 or Laves formation.
The proposed mechanism cannot operate in a composition region where single-phase BCC remains stable at all temperatures or where an intermetallic is the lowest-energy state.
A continuous ordered B2 matrix is associated with low compressive ductility, while reducing B2 continuity can improve ductility.

contradictions.description: The alloy is allowed to be equiatomic, yet avoidance of specific stoichiometric ratios is presented as a reason ordered compounds will not form; no compositional modification or local-chemistry criterion is given to reconcile these statements.

The hypothesis requires grains below 50 nm and predicts 30-45 nm, but the falsification rule rejects the route only when grains exceed 100 nm. Results between 50 and 100 nm would contradict the stated target without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
